clinicalPearls: Arsenic exposure occurs occupationally in smelting, pesticide and wood-preservative work and environmentally through contaminated drinking water, a major public health problem in some regions
Acute poisoning presents with severe gastrointestinal upset including profuse vomiting and 'rice-water' diarrhoea, dehydration, and cardiovascular collapse
Chronic exposure produces characteristic skin changes such as hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles and patchy pigmentation, along with a peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy
Chronic arsenicosis is associated with an increased risk of skin, lung and bladder cancers, so exposed populations need long-term surveillance
A painful, ascending sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy is a hallmark of subacute and chronic toxicity
Diagnosis is supported by measuring arsenic in urine, and in chronic cases hair and nail levels, interpreted alongside the exposure history
Transverse white lines across the nails (Mees' lines) may appear weeks after significant exposure
Management involves stopping exposure, aggressive supportive care in acute poisoning, and use of a chelating agent in significant confirmed toxicity under specialist guidance
reference.pathophysiology: Arsenic exerts toxicity mainly by binding to sulfhydryl groups on enzymes and interfering with cellular energy metabolism, including inhibition of enzymes in the pyruvate and citric acid cycle pathways, and by substituting for phosphate. This impairs oxidative metabolism and generates oxidative stress, damaging the gastrointestinal epithelium, peripheral nerves, skin, and vascular endothelium; genotoxic and epigenetic effects underlie the increased cancer risk with chronic exposure.
additionalDifferentials: Guillain-Barre syndrome and other causes of peripheral neuropathy
Other heavy metal poisoning such as lead or thallium
additionalInvestigations: Spot and 24-hour urinary arsenic measurement (with speciation to exclude dietary organic arsenic)
Hair and nail arsenic levels for chronic exposure assessment
Nerve conduction studies for suspected neuropathy
Full blood count, renal and liver function and ECG in acute toxicity
Skin examination and biopsy where malignancy is suspected
redFlags: MEDICAL EMERGENCY: acute poisoning with severe vomiting and diarrhoea, hypovolaemic shock, or cardiac dysrhythmia including QT prolongation
Rapidly progressive peripheral neuropathy or encephalopathy
New suspicious skin, lung or bladder lesions in chronically exposed individuals
reference.prognosis: With prompt removal from exposure and supportive care, mild to moderate poisoning can recover, though peripheral neuropathy may resolve only slowly and incompletely; severe acute poisoning can be fatal, and chronic exposure carries lasting cancer risk.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing acute poisoning as ordinary gastroenteritis and missing the exposure source
Misinterpreting raised urinary arsenic from recent seafood (organic arsenic) as toxic inorganic exposure
Overlooking contaminated drinking water as an ongoing environmental source
Failing to arrange cancer surveillance in chronically exposed individuals
Attributing neuropathy to other causes without checking exposure
management: Immediate removal from the source of exposure, whether contaminated water or an occupational setting
Chelation therapy with a sulfhydryl-binding agent such as succimer, unithiol or dimercaprol in significant acute or symptomatic poisoning
Aggressive fluid resuscitation and electrolyte replacement for the profuse gastrointestinal losses of acute poisoning
Cardiac monitoring for QT prolongation and arrhythmia with supportive cardiovascular care
Supportive management of the sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy with neuropathic pain agents and physiotherapy
Long-term surveillance for skin, lung and bladder malignancy in chronic arsenicosis
Serial urinary arsenic measurement to confirm falling body burden, alongside public health remediation of contaminated water and occupational controls
